title: Calculus 2
body:
Calculus 2 has two halves. The first finishes integration, because [[CALCULUS 1]] left it
unfinished: differentiation is mechanical and works on every elementary function, and
integration needs a technique chosen to match the integrand. The second half establishes that
an infinite sum can equal a finite number, and once that is granted, a function can be written
as an infinite polynomial.

The connection between the halves is approximation. Calc 1 approximated a curve by a tangent
line, which is one term. This course approximates it by a polynomial of any degree and then
asks whether the approximation survives being taken to infinitely many terms.
[[Linear Approximation]] is the one-term case and [[Taylor Series]] is the same construction
continued, which is why [[Convergence Tests]] is a central note in a course that looks like it
is about integration.

The applications in a CS degree are direct. [[Taylor Series]] is how `sin`, `exp` and `ln` are
actually computed, so the truncation error of a series is the same object as the
representation error in [[Data representation]]. A [[Probability Density Function]] in
[[STATISTICS]] is well defined because an improper integral over the whole line converges
to $1$.

## Topics

### Choosing an integration technique

[[Integration Techniques]] holds the selection table and is the note to read first, because the
skill being taught is recognising which technique the shape of the integrand calls for. The
order to try them is substitution first because it is cheapest, then parts, then partial
fractions when the integrand is a ratio of polynomials, then trigonometric substitution when a
radical of the form $\sqrt{a^2 \pm x^2}$ or $\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}$ appears.

**[[Integration By Parts]]** runs the product rule backwards:

$$
\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du
$$

Choose $u$ so that $du$ is simpler than $u$, which LIATE orders as logarithmic, inverse
trigonometric, algebraic, trigonometric, exponential.

$$
\int x e^x\,dx \quad\text{with } u = x,\; dv = e^x dx
\;=\; x e^x - \int e^x\,dx \;=\; x e^x - e^x + C
$$

The $x$ differentiated down to 1 and the integral that remained was elementary, which is the
first of the two ways the method terminates. The second is that the original integral
reappears and the equation is solved for it, as in $\int e^x \sin x\,dx$ over two rounds. A
choice of $u$ producing neither was the wrong choice. Taking $dv = dx$ handles a lone
logarithm, giving $\int \ln x\,dx = x\ln x - x + C$.

**[[Integration By Partial Fractions]]** splits a rational function into pieces with elementary
antiderivatives:

$$
\frac{1}{(x-1)(x+1)} = \frac{A}{x-1} + \frac{B}{x+1}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad 1 = A(x+1) + B(x-1)
$$

Setting $x = 1$ gives $A = \tfrac12$ and $x = -1$ gives $B = -\tfrac12$, so the integral
becomes $\tfrac12\ln|x-1| - \tfrac12\ln|x+1| + C$. The numerator degree has to fall below the
denominator degree first, so a division step comes before anything else. A repeated linear
factor $(x-a)^k$ contributes $k$ terms, one per power, and an irreducible quadratic contributes
a numerator of the form $Bx + C$.

**[[Integration By Trigonometric Substitution]]** trades $x$ for a [[Trigonometric Function]]
so a Pythagorean identity removes the radical:

```
√(a² - x²)   take x = a sin θ    then √(a² - a²sin²θ) = a cos θ
√(a² + x²)   take x = a tan θ    then the radical becomes a sec θ
√(x² - a²)   take x = a sec θ    then the radical becomes a tan θ
```

Drawing the right triangle is how the answer converts back to $x$ at the end.
[[Trigonometric Integrals]] covers powers of sine, cosine, tangent and secant, using the
odd-power and half-angle strategies.

### Integrals that run to infinity

An [[Improper Integral]] has an infinite limit of integration or an unbounded integrand, and it
is defined as a [[Limit]] of proper integrals:

$$
\int_1^\infty \frac{dx}{x^2} = \lim_{t\to\infty}\int_1^t x^{-2}dx
= \lim_{t\to\infty}\left[-\tfrac{1}{x}\right]_1^t = \lim_{t\to\infty}\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{t}\right) = 1
$$

A region of infinite length has finite area, because the function shrinks fast enough. Change
the exponent to 1 and it does not: $\int_1^\infty \frac{dx}{x}$ gives $\ln t$, which grows
without bound, so the integral diverges and no value can be assigned. In general
$\int_1^\infty x^{-p}dx$ converges exactly when $p > 1$, and near zero the condition reverses,
with $\int_0^1 x^{-p}dx$ converging exactly when $p < 1$. Both are the comparison every other
improper integral is judged against.

### Applications of integration

Every application in this block runs the same three steps: cut the quantity into thin slices,
write what one slice contributes, and integrate that expression over the range. The technique
is the [[Riemann Sum]] from Calc 1 applied to something other than area.

[[Solids of Revolution]] rotates a region around an axis. Disks and washers slice
perpendicular to the axis, so a slice is a circle of radius $f(x)$ and thickness $dx$
contributing $\pi f(x)^2\,dx$. Cylindrical shells slice parallel to the axis, so a slice is a
thin tube contributing $2\pi(\text{radius})(\text{height})\,dx$. The choice between them is
whichever avoids solving the curve for the other variable.

[[Arc Length]] gives three formulas for one quantity, the Cartesian
$\int \sqrt{1 + (f'(x))^2}\,dx$, the parametric
$\int \sqrt{(dx/dt)^2 + (dy/dt)^2}\,dt$, and the polar
$\int \sqrt{r^2 + (dr/d\theta)^2}\,d\theta$. All three are $\int \sqrt{dx^2+dy^2}$ with a
different variable factored out, which is Pythagoras on a slice so short it is straight.

[[Applications of Integration]] covers work, hydrostatic force, centroids and centres of mass
by the same procedure. Work is $\int F(x)\,dx$, and the difficulty in every physical
application is identifying what varies with the slice variable, whether that is the force, the
distance moved or the density.

The [[Double Integral]] integrates over a region of the plane, giving the volume under a
surface, and it is the point where one curve and one axis stop describing the region.

### Sequences and series

A [[Sequence]] is an infinite list of numbers and converges when its terms approach a single
value. An [[Infinite Series]] is the sum of a sequence, and it is defined as the limit of its
partial sums:

$$
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{2^n}
\quad\text{has partial sums } 1,\; 1.5,\; 1.75,\; 1.875,\; \ldots \to 2
$$

The sum is 2 because the partial sums converge to 2, and no infinite addition is performed at
any point. Confusing the sequence of terms with the sequence of partial sums is the most
common error in the block, and the harmonic series is why it matters: the terms of
$\sum 1/n$ approach zero and the partial sums grow without bound, passing 7.48 by $n = 1000$
and reaching any target eventually.

That example fixes the $n$th term test in place. Terms failing to approach zero proves the
series diverges. Terms approaching zero decides nothing.

Two families have known answers. A geometric series $\sum_{n=0}^\infty ar^n$ converges exactly
when $|r| < 1$, to $\frac{a}{1-r}$, and it is the common series whose sum has a closed form
where every other test returns only a verdict. A $p$-series $\sum \frac{1}{n^p}$ converges
exactly when $p > 1$, matching the improper integral threshold above, because the integral
test is the proof.

[[Convergence Tests]] holds the selection table for all seven, and choosing one is the exam
skill:

| Test | Use when the terms contain |
|---|---|
| $n$th term | anything, as a first check for divergence |
| Geometric or $p$-series | a recognisable standard form |
| Comparison or limit comparison | a ratio of polynomials |
| Ratio | factorials or $n$th powers |
| Root | an $n$th power throughout |
| Integral | a term that is easy to integrate |
| Alternating series | alternating signs |

A limit $L < 1$ from the ratio or root test gives convergence, $L > 1$ gives divergence, and
$L = 1$ means that test failed and another is needed. Absolute convergence implies
convergence, and the converse fails: $\sum \frac{(-1)^n}{n}$ converges conditionally, and
rearranging its terms can produce any sum at all, which is what gives the distinction
practical consequences.

### Power series and Taylor series

A [[Power Series]] has an $x$ in it and converges on an interval centred at $a$, which is the
single point $a$, all of $\mathbb{R}$, or a radius $R$ the ratio test produces. The two
endpoints fall outside the ratio test and are checked separately.

[[Taylor Series]] is the power series a function generates from its own derivatives at one
point:

$$
f(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}(x-a)^n
$$

Every coefficient is a derivative at a single point, so the behaviour of an analytic function
everywhere is encoded in what it is doing at one place. [[Maclaurin Series]] is the case
$a = 0$, and five expansions cover most of the work:

$$
e^x = \sum \frac{x^n}{n!}, \quad
\sin x = \sum \frac{(-1)^n x^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}, \quad
\cos x = \sum \frac{(-1)^n x^{2n}}{(2n)!}
$$
$$
\frac{1}{1-x} = \sum x^n \;\; (|x|<1), \qquad
\ln(1+x) = \sum \frac{(-1)^{n+1}x^n}{n}
$$

Everything else is built from those by substituting, differentiating, integrating or
multiplying. Truncating one is how a computer evaluates a transcendental function:

```
e^0.1  ≈  1 + 0.1 + 0.005 + 0.000167  =  1.1051667
true value                             =  1.1051709
four terms, and the error is under 5 × 10⁻⁶
```

The alternating series error bound, where the error is smaller than the first omitted term,
tells the implementation when to stop adding terms.

### Parametric and polar

[[Parametric Equations]] describe a curve by where a point sits at time $t$, which allows a
curve to loop, cross itself and have vertical tangents, none of which a function $y = f(x)$
can do. The slope is $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}$, and the second derivative is
$\frac{d}{dt}\!\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right) \big/ \frac{dx}{dt}$, which differs from dividing
the two second derivatives.

[[Polar Coordinates]] locate a point by distance and angle, converting through
$x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$, $r^2 = x^2+y^2$ and $\tan\theta = y/x$ with the quadrant
checked. Area in polar form sums circular sectors:

$$
A = \frac{1}{2}\int r^2\,d\theta
$$

where $\tfrac12 r^2 d\theta$ is the area of a thin wedge. These are the formulas
[[Polar Form]] in [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] uses on a complex number, applied here to a point in the
plane.

### Differential equations

[[Differential Equations]] appear here as an application of integration. Separation of
variables collects the $y$ terms on one side and integrates both:

$$
\frac{dy}{dx} = ky
\;\Rightarrow\; \int \frac{dy}{y} = \int k\,dx
\;\Rightarrow\; \ln|y| = kx + C
\;\Rightarrow\; y = Ae^{kx}
$$

That derives exponential growth from a statement about rates, and it is the model behind
population growth, radioactive decay and compound interest. The integrating factor handles linear
first-order equations, and second-order homogeneous equations reduce to the roots of a
characteristic polynomial. [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]] owns the full treatment, including
[[Homogeneous ODE]], [[Non-Homogeneous ODE]], [[Undetermined Coefficients]] and
[[Cauchy-Euler]]. Solving an ODE ends in an integral, so every technique above is a
prerequisite, and [[Power Series]] solutions are the method used when none of them applies.

### Multivariable calculus

The final block introduces functions of several variables and stops. A function of two
variables is a surface, a [[Partial Derivative]] is the ordinary derivative taken with the
other variables held constant, the [[Gradient]] collects the partials into a vector pointing
uphill, and the [[Multivariable Chain Rule]] is the [[Chain Rule]] summed over every path a
dependence can take. [[Multivariable Calculus]] and [[Vector Calculus]] in
[[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]] develop all of it, along with [[Multiple Integration]] for triples.

## Related courses

- [[CALCULUS 1]] is the prerequisite and the handoff is exact. It stops at
  [[U-Substitution]], where [[Integration Techniques]] resumes. [[Taylor Series]] continues
  [[Linear Approximation]] past its first term, every convergence question is a [[Limit]]
  question, and [[Riemann Sum]] is the construction every application here re-runs with a
  different slice.
- [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]] owns the two blocks introduced here, in
  [[Differential Equations]] and the multivariable material.
- [[STATISTICS]] normalises a [[Probability Density Function]] with an
  [[Improper Integral]], evaluates the exponential and gamma densities by
  [[Integration By Parts]], and computes [[Average Value]] as a definite integral.
- [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] writes a function as an infinite sum in a
  different basis. [[Taylor Series]] uses powers of $(x-a)$ and describes behaviour near one
  point, while [[Fourier Series]] uses sines and cosines and describes a whole interval.
  [[Orthogonal Functions]] makes the shared idea precise, and its coefficients are integrals
  evaluated with the techniques above.
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] uses the same trigonometry in [[Polar Form]] that
  [[Polar Coordinates]] uses here.
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] has [[Vector Norm]] as the discrete version
  of the arc length and $L^2$ integrals here, and [[Wavelet Transform]] as a basis expansion
  with the same convergence bookkeeping.
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] computes transcendental functions by truncating a Taylor
  series, and the leftover error sits alongside the representation error in
  [[Data representation]].
- [[MACHINE LEARNING]] has [[Gradient Descent]] converging for the same reasons a [[Sequence]]
  does, and the distinction between linear and quadratic convergence is a statement about the
  ratio of successive errors, which is the ratio test applied to an optimiser.
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] uses the geometric series to get
  $\sum_{i=0}^{\log n} \frac{n}{2^i} = O(n)$, which is where the merge work in [[Merge Sort]]
  and the other [[Recursion|recursive]] halving analyses land.
